Mansplaining
MAN-splayn-ing
noun / verb (Millennial slang)
A blend of man and explaining, for a man explaining something to a woman in a condescending way, especially something she already knows better than he does. The word appeared online in 2008, shortly after the writer Rebecca Solnit’s essay "Men Explain Things to Me" (2008), though Solnit did not coin it. The New York Times listed it among words of the year in 2010; online dictionaries added it by 2014. It spawned many blends and became a staple of 2010s gender debate; critics argue it is often used to dismiss any man’s explanation by his sex.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To mansplain is to explain something condescendingly to a woman, assuming she knows less because she is a woman, often when she knows more. The word names a real fault and also carries a framework. The Christian observation: the fault it names is a sin Scripture condemns in anyone. "A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself" (Pro 18:2). "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Pro 18:13). "Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19). A man who talks down to his wife, sister, or coworker, assuming ignorance, is proud, and pride is not masculinity. Scripture’s women include Deborah, who judged Israel; Abigail, whose wisdom saved David from bloodshed; and Priscilla, who with her husband "expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly" to the learned Apollos (Act 18:26). Husbands are told to honour their wives "as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life" (1Pe 3:7), weaker in strength, equal in grace. At the same time, the word comes from a framework that interprets relations between the sexes mainly as a contest of power, and it is often used to silence men simply for being men, or to dismiss the biblical teaching of male headship and pastoral office as condescension. A father teaches his son: listen before you speak, never assume a woman knows less, and lead with humility. He teaches his daughter: speak your knowledge with grace, and do not let a slogan teach you that every man who explains something is your enemy.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial-era slang (2008; after Solnit’s essay) for a man’s condescending explanation to a woman; it names real pride Scripture condemns (Pro 18:2; Jas 1:19), within a power-contest framework often used to silence men and dismiss biblical headship.

MANSPLAINING, n.; MANSPLAIN, v. (Millennial-era slang, 2008–present; blend of man + explaining) Explaining something to a woman in a condescending manner, often assuming her ignorance. Spawned blends such as -splaining.

Webster (1828), root explain: EXPLAIN, verb transitive [Latin explano; ex and planus, plain, open, smooth.] To make plain, manifest or intelligible; to clear of obscurity; to expound; to illustrate by discourse, or by notes. The first business of a preacher is to explain his text. Notes and comments are intended to explain the scriptures.

Decode for parents: teach sons to listen first and daughters not to read every male explanation as an attack.

Key Scripture

Pro 18:2 — "A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself."

Pro 18:13 — "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him."

Jas 1:19 — "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:"

Act 18:26 — "And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly."

1Pe 3:7 — "Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered."

Modern Corruption

Mansplaining names real male pride that Scripture condemns, but carries a framework that treats the sexes as rivals and is often used to silence men and discredit biblical headship.

expand to see more

The corruption is in the framework more than the fault. Condescension is sin, and Christian men should repent of it wherever it appears. But the word was built within a view that sees every interaction between men and women through the lens of power, and in practice it can be used to dismiss any man’s speech by his sex alone, which is itself a kind of prejudice. It is also often aimed at the biblical teaching that men lead in the home and the church, as though headship were merely a habit of talking down.

The recovery is humility in both directions. Biblical headship is servant leadership, modelled on Christ, who washed feet; it has no room for arrogance. Biblical womanhood includes wisdom, teaching of children and younger women, and the courage to speak truth, as Abigail did. Teach the young to listen before speaking, to respect knowledge wherever it is found, and to reject both male arrogance and the slogans that make the sexes enemies.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Man + explain (Latin explanare, to make level, plain) → 2008 mansplaining (after Solnit’s essay) → 2010 NYT words of the year → 2014 dictionaries.
